title: The Leader's Greatest Return: Attracting, Developing, and Multiplying Leaders
author: John C. Maxwell (see Source Notes — not Tony Robbins)
summary:
Before anything else: I need to flag a correction. Your catalog lists this as a Tony Robbins book titled "Ask for More / The Leader's Greatest Return." I could not find any Tony Robbins book by either title. "The Leader's Greatest Return: Attracting, Developing, and Multiplying Leaders" is a real, well-documented 2020 book, but it's written by John C. Maxwell, the veteran leadership author, not Tony Robbins — the two authors work in an overlapping space (leadership and personal development publishing) which may explain the mix-up in your library catalog. I also couldn't find any evidence of a real book titled "Ask for More" by either author. Rather than force a Tony Robbins framing onto content that actually belongs to Maxwell, I've written this entry for the confirmed real book — The Leader's Greatest Return by John C. Maxwell — and I'd recommend double-checking your physical copy's cover and author credit to confirm this is indeed the book on your shelf.

With that correction in place: The Leader's Greatest Return is the culmination of Maxwell's decades-long shift in focus from "leading people" to "developing other leaders," representing what he describes as the highest-leverage activity available to anyone in a position of influence. The book's central argument is that leaders create their most lasting impact not through their own direct actions, but by identifying, developing, empowering, and ultimately multiplying other leaders — turning a single leader's capability into a compounding, self-sustaining network of leadership throughout an organization.

Maxwell structures the book as a step-by-step process: creating a "Leadership Table" where potential leaders can be welcomed in and try on leadership responsibility in a low-stakes way; understanding what he calls the seven motivators that drive different people, so leaders can be developed according to what actually moves them rather than a one-size-fits-all approach; using a "10-80-10" method to structure how much oversight and autonomy to give people at different stages of their development; and progressively moving people through stages of attracting, understanding, motivating, equipping, empowering, positioning, and eventually mentoring them to develop leaders of their own — creating a compounding, multi-generational effect Maxwell frames as a leader's truest legacy.

Throughout, Maxwell draws on his own decades of leadership training work — by his own account, growing from developing a handful of leaders in a single organization early in his career to influencing millions of leaders across business, government, and nonprofit sectors worldwide — and illustrates his points with a mix of personal stories and examples of leaders he has personally developed. The book is explicitly framed as a natural extension of his earlier, foundational work The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership, applying those broader leadership principles specifically to the narrower, high-leverage question of how a leader multiplies their impact by building other leaders rather than simply leading followers directly.

sections.title: The Leadership Table
sections.summary:
This opening chapter introduces Maxwell's concept of the "Leadership Table" — a deliberate, structured setting where people who aren't yet leading at a senior level can be invited in, observe how leadership decisions are made, and begin trying on leadership responsibility in a supported, low-risk environment. It argues that most organizations never create such a space, leaving potential leaders to either sink-or-swim in real high-stakes situations or never get the exposure they need at all.

The chapter details practical guidance on who to invite to the table, how to structure the experience so it's genuinely developmental rather than just observational, and how to use it to identify which invitees have real leadership potential worth further investment.

It transitions into the next chapter by establishing that once potential leaders are identified through the Leadership Table, effectively developing them requires understanding what actually motivates each individual person.
keyLessons: Deliberately create low-stakes settings where potential leaders can practice leadership before being placed in high-stakes situations.
The Leadership Table is a tool for identification as much as development — it reveals who has genuine leadership potential.

sections.title: The Seven Motivators
sections.summary:
This chapter presents Maxwell's framework of seven distinct motivators that drive different people — arguing that a leader who tries to motivate everyone the same way will consistently underperform a leader who diagnoses what genuinely moves each individual and adapts their approach accordingly. The chapter walks through how to identify which motivator(s) apply to a given person through observation and direct conversation.

Maxwell uses this framework to argue against generic, one-size-fits-all leadership development programs, instead advocating for individualized development plans built around each person's actual motivational profile.

It hands off to the following chapters on empowerment and team structure by noting that correctly identifying motivation is only useful if paired with a structure that lets people act on it.
keyLessons: Different people are driven by fundamentally different motivators; a single generic approach to motivation underperforms a diagnosed, individualized one.
Take time to directly observe and ask about what motivates specific team members rather than assuming.

sections.title: Team Success — The 10-80-10 Method
sections.summary:
This chapter introduces Maxwell's "10-80-10" method for structuring how a leader supports someone through a task or project: providing focused guidance at the beginning (the first 10%) and end (the final 10%) of a process, while empowering the person to work with real autonomy through the middle 80% without micromanagement. The goal is setting people up for success without stripping them of the ownership that actual development requires.

The chapter details how to apply this structure practically — what kind of guidance belongs in the opening 10%, what kind of course-correction belongs in the closing 10%, and how to resist the urge to intervene during the middle stretch even when it would be faster to just do it yourself.

It leads into the book's later chapters on positioning and reproducing leaders by establishing that empowerment structured this way is what actually builds a person's leadership capability, not just their task completion.
keyLessons: Concentrate hands-on guidance at the start and end of a task, and grant real autonomy through the middle stretch.
Resist micromanaging the middle of a delegated task, even when it feels slower or riskier — that autonomy is what builds real capability.

sections.title: From Developing to Reproducing Leaders
sections.summary:
This later section of the book addresses Maxwell's ultimate argument: the highest level of leadership impact comes not from developing individual leaders but from developing leaders who go on to develop other leaders themselves, creating a compounding, multi-generational effect. He distinguishes between leaders who add value directly and leaders who multiply value by building other value-adders.

The chapter uses examples of specific people Maxwell has personally mentored — including references to leaders he's developed within his own organizations — to illustrate what this reproducing, compounding process looks like in practice over years, not months.

The book closes by framing this reproducing capability as a leader's truest legacy — the return that continues to compound long after the original leader's own direct influence has ended, which gives the book its title.
keyLessons: The highest-leverage leadership activity is developing leaders who go on to develop other leaders, not just developing individual contributors.
A leader's most durable legacy is measured in the leaders they've reproduced, not the direct results they personally achieved.
Create a deliberate, low-stakes "Leadership Table" where potential leaders can practice and be observed before facing high-stakes responsibility.
Diagnose what actually motivates each individual person rather than applying a single, generic motivational approach to everyone.
Use the 10-80-10 method: concentrate guidance at the start and end of a delegated task, and grant real autonomy through the middle.
Resist micromanaging people you've chosen to empower — oversight that never lets go undermines the very development it's meant to produce.
Actively add value to the people you lead, not just extract value from their work.
The highest form of leadership impact is developing leaders who go on to develop other leaders — a compounding, multi-generational effect.
Measure your leadership legacy by the leaders you've reproduced, not just the direct results you personally achieved.
Build systems and habits for mentoring, not just isolated moments of good advice.

quotes.text: In the last twenty-five years, New York Times bestselling author John C. Maxwell has grown from equipping a handful of leaders in one organization to developing millions of business, government, and nonprofit leaders in every country around the world.
The Leadership Table - Create a place where people not yet leading at your level can come, be welcomed and try on leadership.
The 7 Motivators - Review the seven motivators and discover what motivates each person and then lead him or her accordingly.
Team Success - Use the 10-80-10 method to set people up for success and empower them to perform at a high level.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Leadership Table
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A deliberate, structured setting where potential leaders who aren't yet operating at a senior level are invited to observe leadership decisions and practice leadership responsibility in a low-stakes environment, functioning as both a development tool and a way to identify genuine leadership potential.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Seven Motivators
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Maxwell's framework describing seven distinct categories of what drives different people, used to individualize how a leader develops and motivates each person on their team rather than applying one generic approach to everyone.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Developed early in the book, following the Leadership Table chapter.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The 10-80-10 Method
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A delegation and empowerment framework: a leader provides focused, hands-on guidance during the first 10% of a task and the final 10%, while granting real autonomy through the middle 80%, balancing support with genuine ownership.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Level 5 Leadership (Referenced Framework)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Maxwell's broader "5 Levels of Leadership" model (from his earlier work) is referenced throughout as the underlying framework this book builds on — with the book's core argument being that reaching the top level of leadership requires developing other leaders who can themselves reproduce leadership in others.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Referenced throughout, most explicitly in the closing chapters on reproducing leaders.

actionSteps: Identify one person in your organization or team with leadership potential who hasn't yet had a formal opportunity to practice leadership, and create one specific, low-stakes situation this month where they can do so with your support nearby.
Have a direct, explicit conversation with one person you lead about what actually motivates them, rather than assuming it's the same thing that motivates you.

On your next delegated project, explicitly plan your involvement using the 10-80-10 structure: define what guidance you'll give at the start, what you'll check at the end, and commit in advance to staying out of the middle.

Identify one person you're currently developing, and ask them directly what it would take for them to start developing someone else — treat this as the real marker of their growth, not just their own individual performance.
reflectionQuestions: Who in your life or organization is currently developing leadership capability because of your direct investment — and who could you be investing in that you currently aren't?
Where are you currently micromanaging the "middle 80%" of a task you've technically delegated, and what would it take to genuinely let go?
If your leadership legacy were measured only by the leaders you've reproduced, not your own direct achievements, how would that change what you prioritize this year?

points: Because your library catalog attributed this book to Tony Robbins, I want to be direct that this Critical Take applies to the actual, confirmed author, John C. Maxwell — please treat the entry as correctly matched to your physical book only after confirming the cover and author credit yourself.

Maxwell's leadership frameworks (here and across his broader body of work) are presented primarily through personal anecdote and illustrative case examples from his own consulting and speaking career, rather than through independently validated organizational research — readers looking for empirically tested leadership science may want to pair this with more research-driven sources.

The book's examples of successfully developed leaders are drawn heavily from Maxwell's own organizations and personal network, which makes it hard for an outside reader to assess how well the frameworks (the Leadership Table, 10-80-10, the Seven Motivators) generalize outside of Maxwell's own culture-controlled environment.

As the latest in a very long series of Maxwell leadership books built on overlapping core ideas (drawn especially from his foundational The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership and the 5 Levels of Leadership), some reviewers have noted this book covers ground that will feel familiar to longtime readers of his other titles, positioned more as a focused deep-dive on leader-reproduction than an entirely new framework.

whoThisIsFor: Managers, executives, and organizational leaders responsible for succession planning or building a bench of future leaders, especially those already familiar with Maxwell's broader leadership frameworks.
whenToReadThis: When you're moving from an individual-leadership role into a role responsible for developing other leaders — a promotion, a growing team, or a succession-planning process.

authorBio.name: John C. Maxwell
authorBio.bio:
John C. Maxwell is an American author, speaker, and pastor widely recognized as one of the most influential leadership development writers of the modern era, having authored dozens of bestselling books on leadership over more than four decades. His work is built heavily on frameworks he's developed and refined through his own organizations, which train and certify leadership coaches and speakers around the world.

His earlier book, The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership, is considered one of the foundational texts of the modern leadership-development genre and remains one of his most widely referenced works. Maxwell has stated that his own focus shifted over his career from leading followers directly to developing other leaders, a shift that The Leader's Greatest Return represents the culmination of.

sourceNotes: Web searches for a Tony Robbins book titled "Ask for More" or "The Leader's Greatest Return" returned no matching results; "The Leader's Greatest Return: Attracting, Developing, and Multiplying Leaders" was consistently and repeatedly confirmed as a 2020 John C. Maxwell book across Amazon, Goodreads, and Maxwell's own blog, which is why this entry was written for that confirmed book rather than forcing a Tony Robbins framing onto it. Chapter structure (Leadership Table, Seven Motivators, 10-80-10 method) verified against the book's official publisher description and a detailed Goodreads review referencing specific chapters; exact chapter numbering and the full seven-motivator list and complete "attracting/developing/positioning" stage sequence could not be fully verified in the sources reviewed, so those specifics are presented at the level of confirmed theme rather than a guaranteed verbatim table of contents. Please verify your physical copy's actual title and author before treating this entry as final.
